Figure 2. Teal starts the axis; blue steps are GH and IGF-1 signalling and drug blocks. Red bar marks a blocked signal; red outcome: acromegaly symptoms improve.

skipped.text: Prolactin: dopamine is the brake on prolactin, shown on the next slide.
Section transition.
Section 02: thyroid and antithyroid drugs.
Figure 6: Iodide trapping, organification, coupling and peripheral conversion.
Methimazole is first-line for most patients and is avoided in the first trimester.
Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets; the next two slides show the mechanism and the sequence.
Figure 7: Four drugs, four targets: PTU blocks synthesis, iodine blocks release (after PTU), propranolol blunts symptoms, steroids blunt conversion.
This case reinforces Figure 6 and the sequencing point from the prior slide — a good checkpoint for whether the mechanism actually landed, not just the drug names.
"Why must iodine come after the thionamide?" Answer: iodine first provides substrate for new hormone.

Section 03: adrenal drugs.
Figure 8: The steroid binds the cytoplasmic receptor, enters the nucleus, and changes transcription; NF-kB driven cytokines are repressed.
Figure 9: Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH.
Enzyme blockers (ketoconazole, metyrapone) lower cortisol.
Figure 10: Receptor blockers (mifepristone, spironolactone) leave hormone levels high.
